Carbon fiber (CF) reinforced polyphenylene sulfide (PPS) composites have garnered significant interest across industries such as automotive, aerospace, and medicine due to their superior corrosion, fatigue, and impact resistance, alongside their adaptability to diverse manufacturing techniques and their potential for long-term storage and recyclability at ambient temperatures [15].

Significantly, the utilization of sizing agents has attracted considerable research attention due to their pivotal role in maintaining the integrity of CF while simultaneously enhancing their processability and adhesion to resins.
Sizing agents for CF are typically classified into thermoplastic and thermosetting categories, with thermosetting agents predominantly used as protective coatings in commercial CF applications.

However, the integration of thermosetting sizing agents into thermoplastic composites introduces several questions: (1) their restricted thermal stability, which may result in premature decomposition at temperatures below the composite's processing temperature (e.g. 335 C for PPS), potentially inducing a debonding effect that impairs the composite's performance; and (2) the compatibility between thermosetting sizing agents and thermoplastic matrices is poor, which can adversely affect the interfacial properties between CF and the resin matrix [1921].
The sizing agent endows carbon fibers with tunable processing performances, preserving their strand integrity while ensuring effective yarn spreadability.

It is imperative to acknowledge that the effectiveness of sizing agents in augmenting the interfacial properties of CF reinforced thermoplastic composites, as well as the processability of CF, is contingent upon the viscosity of the agents.
Given the direct correlation between viscosity and molecular weight, investigating the molecular weight of sizing agents is pivotal for optimizing their performance.
Researchers have extensively investigated thermoplastic sizing agents to enhance the interface properties and processability of CF in composite materials.
For instance, Yan et al. [28] synthesized an aqueous aminoethyl piperazine-polyamide (AEPPA) and assessed its impact on the surface properties of CF.
However, to our knowledge, the influence of molecular weight of thermoplastic sizing agent on CF processability and composite properties has never been sufficiently documented.

Finetuning the molecular weight of sizing agents was essential for enhancing CF processability and the interfacial characteristics in thermoplastic composites, given the fact the molecular weight of conventional thermoplastic sizing agent would be much larger than that of the prepolymer for thermosetting sizing agent, and the duration of sizing process in industrial production line is rather short.

This study explored the synthesis of water-soluble PAAs in aqueous medium, yielding three variants with distinct molecular weights by modulating monomer ratios, and prepared CF/PPS composites with these different PAAs sizing agents.

The analysis was centered on the investigation on how the molecular weight variation of PAAs (the molecular weights of PAAs were determined to be 1000 g/mol, 4003 g/mol, and 23,539 g/mol) affected the processability of CF, the interfacial characteristics, and the mechanical performance of the ensuing CF/PPS composites.
The synthesized PAAs exhibited several benefits, such as thermal stability, eco-friendliness, facile synthesis, and enhanced impregnation.

Since the PAAs sizing agent would be thermally imidized into PI during the molding process of CF/PPS composites, an intentional heat treatment was performed in an oven at 320 °C for 2 h to mimic the thermal imidization during processing for all three sizing agents, named as L-PI, M-PI and H-PI.

Nickel-based superalloys are widely used as critical materials for hotend components in aerospace and energy production areas owing to their excellent mechanical properties, thermal stability and oxidation resistance [1,2].
However, conventional manufacturing processes are increasingly difficult to meet the demand for lightweight and integrated fabrication of intricate components [3].

On the one hand, most of the existing commercial alloys are unable to accommodate the spatially variable temperature fields and ultrafast cooling rates during AM fabrication, and thus exhibit significant cracking [79].

On the other hand, the heterogeneous microstructure and the defects generated by non-equilibrium solidification make it difficult for alloys to achieve the performance levels obtained by conventional manufacturing methods, especially under long-term service conditions [5,1012].
Optimizing the composition of existing alloys to improve their printability has recently attracted extensive attention in the AM field.

Substantial researches utilizing atomic probe technology, non-equilibrium Scheil model, and hot crack sensitivity index theory have confirmed that the segregation of Zr, B, Si, Mn, etc. elements increase the cracking tendency of nickel-based superalloys and that the reduction or removal of these elements can effectively inhibit cracking [1517].
For instance, Després et al. [13] achieved crack-free fabrication of IN738LC alloy by removing Zr from the alloy composition.

However, it is well accepted that the existence of trace alloying elements such as s Zr, $\mathrm { Z r , }$ B in nickel-based superalloys improves grain boundary strength and reduces the rate of grain boundary diffusion, thereby greatly improving creep resistance and notch sensitivity [1922].

Therefore, the contradiction between the improved printability of AM-fabricated nickel-based superalloys and the degradation of long-term service mechanical properties caused by the reduction in the content of grain boundary-acting elements needs to be overcome for composition optimization.

Although the addition of 1 wt% Zr eliminated cracking in nickel-based superalloys and enabled outstanding room temperature mechanical properties, Zr is usually present as a trace alloying element (generally < 0.2 wt%) in existing nickel-based superalloys.

Excessive Zr content can lead to increased solubility of carbon in the matrix, resulting in lamellar carbide precipitation, which can serve a favorable position for creep voids and crack propagation [26].
Moreover, it has also been reported that the Ni-Zr phase can reduce the stress-rupture life of cast nickel-based superalloys [27].

However, extraordinary properties have been reported by modulation of elements beyond the constant amount in previous work, such as Zhang et al. added 8.5 wt% of Cu to pure Ti and achieved the transformation of columnar to equiaxial grains in AM-fabricated samples and increased the strength by 270 MPa [23].
Choudhuri et al. achieved a 600 % improvement in the creep life of Mg-Nd alloy by introducing 0.4 at% zinc [28].

Therefore, it remains to be further clarified that Zr additions beyond the norm may have a negative/beneficial effect on the creep lifetime, oxidation resistance and microstructural stability of AM-fabricated nickel-based superalloys in long-term service at elevated temperatures.
Two types of the nickel-based superalloys Haynes 230 and Haynes 230AM (1 wt% Zr added) were used for comparative verification of the above-mentioned properties changes.

Benefitting from the addition of $\mathbf { Z r , }$ the Haynes 230AM alloy exhibits excellent creep and oxidation resistance, and still maintains stable mechanical properties after long-term thermal exposure.
These results provide important guidance for facilitating the compositional design and engineering application of similar alloys suitable for AM with excellent properties and printability.

AM is gaining popularity for part manufacturing that can directly compete with traditional manufacturing methods such as subtractive, joining, or formative (Conner et al., 2014).
As of 2016, the market value of AM was \~\$6.06 billion with an estimated potential growth of 4.3 times by the year 2022 (Wohlers, 2017).
The adaptation of these technologies continues to expand into multiple application markets, driving the AM industry towards the qualification of more metal alloys for use with PBF processes.
Nickel-based superalloys such as Inconel 718 and 625 have seen widespread adoption in multiple fields due to the alloys' multipurpose capabilities and range of applications.

While conventional manufacturing of components using these high-performance alloys has been difficult due to excessive tool wear and low material removal rates, the use of powder-based AM technologies can remove these constraints while also improving lead times and reducing manufacturing costs (Costes et al., 2007; Buchbinder et al., 2011).
Inconel 625 consists mostly of nickel (61.0 wt%) and chromium (21.5 wt%) with other alloying elements including molybdenum, niobium, and iron (Eiselstein and Tillack, 1991).

For PBF AM, the chemical requirements (in wt%) for Inconel 625 include: Cr at 20-23%, Mo at 8- 10%, Niobium at 3.15-4.15%, and maximum wt% for C at 0.10, Mn at 0.50, Si at 0.50, P at 0.015, S at 0.015, Co at 1.00, Ti at 0.40, Al at 0.40 and Fe at 5.00, with the remainder of Ni (ASTM International, 2014a).

Inconel 625 has found widespread and diverse applications in the aerospace, marine service and petrochemical industries due to the excellent combination of strength, resulting from age hardening, at both ambient and elevated temperatures, as well as corrosion resistance (Rai et al., 2004).
Finally, Inconel 625 has seen widespread use in marine service and in the nuclear industry due to the ability of the material to resist sea water corrosion (Hu et al., 2010).

Inconel 625 components have been manufactured using several conventional manufacturing processes such as casting, powder metallurgy, spray forming, weld overlaying and co-extrusion of piping components (Song and Nakata, 2010).
As the demand and growth of AM continues, fabrication using AM with Inconel 625 has emerged as a promising method for part production.

Therefore, the focus of this research is a characterization of Inconel 625 components fabricated by three different powder-bedbased AM technologies with an emphasis on comparing the mechanical properties of components manufactured with each technology.

A thorough material characterization of Inconel 625 parts fabricated using these three technologies was performed followed by a mechanical properties comparison for components built in two orientations: horizontal (X) and vertical (Z).
Results were then compared to ASTM standards established for AM fabrication of Inconel 625.

Binder Jetting is defined as an "additive manufacturing process in which a liquid bonding agent is selectively deposited to join powder materials," according to ISO/ASTM 52900 (ASTM International, 2015).

The final step in the creation of a dense part, sintering, is performed on the brown body at elevated temperatures necessary to initiate sintering, usually ranging from 0.5 to 0.8 times the melting point $( \mathrm { T } _ { \mathrm { m } , }$ 12901350 °C for Inconel 625), allowing the powder particles to fuse together (Anon., 2018).
As per ISO/ASTM 52900, powder bed fusion is defined as "an additive manufacturing process in which thermal energy selectively fuses regions of a powder bed" (ASTM International, 2015).

The process takes place in a vacuum environment $( \sim 1 0 ^ { 4 }$ Torr) and at a high powder bed temperature of \~ 850 C for Inconel 625, producing parts with reduced build up of residual stress (Murr et al., 2012).

EPBF can process a vast variety of materials and Arcam, the manufacturer of the EPBF equipment used here, has commercially released parameters for materials such as the titanium alloy Ti6Al4V, Ti6Al4V ELI, titanium grade 2, Arcam ASTM F75 cobaltchrome, and nickel-based superalloy Inconel 718 (Arcam, 2011).
The LPBF fabrication process is completed in an inert gas environment (argon or nitrogen), differing from EPBF.
Commercially available parameters for LPBF enable for fabrication of parts at layer heights that usually range from 20 to 70 µm.
LPBF technology has achieved success in the fabrication of titanium alloys, stainless steel, tool steels, aluminum, cobalt chrome and nickel based alloys (SLM Solutions, 2018).

LPBF parts were fabricated in an SLM Solutions 125 HL system (Lübeck, Germany) available in-house using commercially available parameters specifically developed by SLM Solutions GmbH for processing the Inconel 625 alloy at 30 µm layers.

Using each technology, round bars were built in two orientations (i.e. horizontal or X direction, and vertical or Z direction, as referred in Fig. 1) for evaluation and testing of mechanical properties.
Flow rates for the powders were determined following ASTM Standard B213-13 (ASTM International, 2014c).
Characterization of properties for powder-bed-based fabricated Inconel 625 was determined by the following specifications and standards.
The average apparent density for binder jetting printed parts increased from 96.5% to 98.3% once post-processing (HIPing) was performed.

Murr et al. showed that EPBF fabricated Inconel alloys, such as 625 and 718, exhibit directional growth of precipitates within the melt zones (Murr, 2015).
Further, Amato et al. demonstrated a change in the microstructure of the components after HIPing, which induced the formation of equiaxed grains and of annealing twins (Amato et al., 2012).

The microstructure was unaltered under aging at $7 0 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for 24 h, but under solutioning at $1 1 5 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for 2 h, or a combination of solutioning and aging using the previous parameters, did result in recrystallization of grains ranging from 10 to 90 µm in size (Marchese et al., 2018).

Results of mechanical testing for the three technologies were compared to the ASTM standard F3056-14 as this specification provides a baseline for components produced by AM technologies to meet mechanical properties equivalent to those of forged and/or wrought nickel alloy products (ASTM International, 2014a).
All three technologies surpassed the minimum requirement set by the ASTM F3056-14 standard (0.485 GPa in both the X and Z build orientations).

A similar behavior was noted in Z orientation fabricated samples.
The results obtained in this manuscript show that HIPing of binder jetting printed parts enabled higher strength values compared to other reported values for Inconel 625 in the aged condition.
Marchese et al. showed increases in YS and UTS for aged Inconel 625 that had been processed using LPBF.
They showed that under an aging schedule of 700 °C for 24 h, the YS and UTS were 1024 ± 54 MPa and 1222 ± 56 MPa, respectively with a ductility of 23% ± 1%.

The mechanical processed components may result in alloy segregation stringers, leading to phases with alignment along a specific orientation, which in turn lead to weak paths during deformation (Blake, 1985).

The mechanical testing results indicated that all three technologies were able to surpass the minimum values for UTS, % elongation, and YS that are required by the ASTM standard F3056-14, achieving equivalent properties to wrought Inconel 625 for the X build orientation specimens.

While this study only considered static mechanical properties and metallurgical features, other variables also need to be taken into account to appropriately select a manufacturing process for a given application.
Although additional research is required, this study can be used to assist companies with considering powder-bed-based technologies as alternative metal fabrication processes to conventional methods.

The global demand for advanced materials has surged as industries increasingly prioritize sustainability and performance under challenging environmental conditions.
However, modern infrastructure and manufacturing needs for advanced alloys extend beyond just their mechanical strength.

With growing concerns over the longevity and structural integrity of materials, especially in aggressive environments, there is a pressing demand for UHSSs that not only excel in terms of their mechanical performance but also offer robust resistance to corrosion.
Microbial corrosion, or microbiologically influenced corrosion (MIC), poses a significant threat to the durability of metals and alloys across various industries [47].
These industries often involve environments rich in water and nutrients that support SRB growth, leading to severe material degradation and safety risks.

Various types of stainless steels with superior corrosion resistance, such as 316 L [1517], 2205 duplex stainless steel [18,19], 321 stainless steel [20] and 304 stainless steel [21,22], are reported to be susceptible to the SRB-induced corrosion.
As the global push for sustainability continues, designing materials that can withstand microbial threats while maintaining superior mechanical properties is a key challenge.
In the above context, integrating the alloying elements such as Cu that are inherently antibacterial into UHSSs has emerged as a promising solution [2729].

This approach aligns with the broader goal of creating long-lasting, eco-friendly materials, as the ability to resist microbial attacks directly reduces the need for frequent maintenance, replacements, and the use of environmentally harmful chemical inhibitors.

Although recent advances in material design have sought to address these issues individually, there remains a clear gap in the simultaneously enhancing mechanical strength, corrosion resistance, and antibacterial properties.

Crystalline anisotropy and the spirit of the crystal plasticity finite-element method

This phenomenon is due to the anisotropy of the elastic tensor and to the orientation dependence of the activation of the crystallographic deformation mechanisms (dislocations, twins, martensitic transformations).

A consequence of crystalline anisotropy is that the associated mechanical phenomena such as shape change, crystallographic texture, strength, strain hardening, deformation-induced surface roughening and damage are also orientation dependent.

Therefore, a theory of the mechanical properties of crystals must include, first, the crystallographic and anisotropic nature of those mechanisms that create shear, and second, the orientation(s) of the crystal(s) studied relative to the applied boundary conditions (e.g. loading axis, rolling plane).

Early approaches to describe anisotropic plasticity under simple boundary conditions have considered these aspects, such as, for instance, the Sachs [3], Taylor [4], BishopHill [5,6] or Kröner [7] formulations.
The essential step which renders the deformation kinematics of this approach a crystal plasticity formulation is the fact that the velocity gradient is written in dyadic form.
This allows one to implement constitutive laws that treat mechanical size effects in conjunction with local orientation gradients [24].

This point is relevant for size-dependent plasticity modeling, as the polarized portions of dislocation arrays (which are often conceptually treated as GNDs),1 such as anticipated in many size effect models, must necessarily coincide with orientation gradients [210].
This approach uses crystal plasticity simulations instead of complicated mechanical tests that are required for fitting yield surface coefficients [217].
CPFE formulations can be either fully integrated into FE codes or implemented as user-defined subroutines into commercially available solvers.

In these steels, alternatively, metastable austenite phase can also be introduced, which can exhibit twinning [8,9] or martensitic transformation [8], leading to increased ductility [10].

Compared to the aging treatments, reversion treatments are carried away at higher temperatures, e.g., at \~600 °C [15].

Significant strength reductions can take place due to the reversion treatment (e.g., from 1.5 GPa to <1 GPa) [6,15], which is generally known to be attributed to the coarsening of precipitate, introduction of the austenite  a phase expected to be softer than the martensite, and recovery of dislocations [15,19].

This would in turn lead to two prepositions regarding the effect of the high reversion temperatures: (i) it should be instead the martensite relaxation processes which are more critical for softening (rather than the austenite fraction introduced); and that (ii) optimal precipitation states are likely missed, due to extended precipitate coarsening effect [14,15].
Based on these points, we propose a design approach here for the introduction of nanolaminate austenite while limiting the softening.

This strategy relies on reducing the extent of reversion-induced martensite relaxation, and of precipitate overaging, by increasing the austenite reversion kinetics; and slowing down the kinetics of precipitation coarsening.

To realize strategy (i), different processes such as cold [25,29] or warm rolling [30,31] can be applied to increase the heterogeneous nucleation spots and thereby accelerate the phase formation, however, the increased defect density can also accelerate diffusion and precipitate coarsening [32].

To date, imine-linked COFs have dominated the development of COFderived protonic electrolytes because of their straightforward synthesis and high crystallinity.
Their applicability is therefore limited to solid-state proton batteries, which require good protonconducting performance under ambient conditions.

text: As a result, few COF-derived solid electrolytes have been explored for proton battery applications [26, 27].
Specifically, zwitterions bearing sulfobetaine groups have shown great promise in enhancing proton conductiviy[29].

Additionally, the sulfonic acid groups embedded within sulfobetaine functionalities can dissociate more effectively under the local electrostatic field generated by neighboring quaternary ammonium sites, thereby accelerating proton transfer.

These attributes suggest that zwitterionic functionalization represents a promising route to overcoming the limited proton conductivity of COFs under ambient conditions and to expanding their utility in proton batteries.

Herein, we present the design of a solid protonic electrolyte that was fabricated by incorporating phosphoric acid into the channels of a robust zwitterionic vinylene-linked COF functionalized with sulfobetaine moieties.

Phosphoric acid (PA) was incorporated into the COFs by mechanically grinding the COFs with varying amounts of PA, resulting in a series of composites denoted as PA@ZVCOF-X and PA@NVCOF-X (X = 40, 60, and 80, representing the mass percentage of PA).
A significant difference in PA-loading capacity was observed between the two COFs.
This observed difference between the two COFs is attributed to their different affinities for PA, as supported by contact angle measurements shown in Figure 2b.
PA droplets spread more readily on ZVCOF, suggesting its higher acidophilicity, which can be ascribed to the high electronegativity of the sulfobetaine groups (Figure S6).
PA revealed diminished crystallinity, supported by the disappearance of characteristic diffraction peaks of COFs.

text: The exceptional chemical robustness of ZVCOF was further confirmed by its retained crystallinity after immersion in 12 M HCl or 12 M NaOH for 48 h (Figure S8). $\Nu _ { 2 }$ adsorption-desorption measurements at 77 K further validated the successful infiltration of PA into the pores of COFs (Figure 2c,d), as the porosity of both COFs significantly decreased following PA loading.

PA@ZVCOF-X $( X = 4 0 – 8 0 )$ exhibited very low BET surface areas $( 9 . 6 { - } 2 6 . 3 \mathrm { m } ^ { 2 } \mathrm { g } ^ { - 1 } )$ and pore volumes $( 0 . 0 0 1 { - } 0 . 0 1 \mathrm { c m } ^ { 3 } \mathbf { g } ^ { - 1 } )$ .

As the PA loading was increased from 40 wt% to 60 wt% in ZvCOF, the proton conductivity of the COF composite doubled across measured temperatures, with PA@ZVCOF-60 achieving proton conductivities of $2 . 1 6 \times 1 0 ^ { - 2 } \mathrm { S c m ^ { - 1 } }$ at 298 K, and $7 . 2 2 \times 1 0 ^ { - 2 } \mathrm { S c m ^ { - 1 } }$ at 413 K.

Increasing the PA content to 60 wt% led to a 23 orders of magnitude improvement, yet the resulting conductivity remained significantly lower than that of the composites based on ZVCOF.

text: In addition to its high proton conductivity, PA@ZVCOF-80 exhibited remarkable long-term proton conduction stability, maintaining consistently high proton conductivity over extended operation periods (Figure S27).

Overall, PA@ZVCOF-X $( X = 4 0 – 8 0 )$ containing the zwitterionic COF exhibited low activation energies in the range of 0.12.1   c  e e0., that proton transport occurs primarily via the Grotthuss-type hopping mechanism [39].
Notably, a ZVCOF sample with a lower PA loading of 20 wt% (PA@ZVCOF-20) was also synthesized and showed a substantially higher $E _ { a }$ of 0.49 eV (Figure S28).
For the ZVCOF-based system, the RDF between H atoms of PA and O atoms of the sulfonate groups [H(PA)-O(ZVCOF)] showed prentstn a 1.00 nd .7 , diive interactions.
Given its exceptional proton conductivity, PA@ZVCOF-80 was further investigated as a solid protonic electrolyte for proton battery applications.

text: PA@ZVCOF-80 was mixed with a small amount (4 wt%) of polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) binder and processed into a membrane by rolling.
The resulting membrane exhibits remarkable thermal stability (Figure S29), good mechanical flexibility, and can be easily bent or crimped without damage (Figure S30).

After confirming the successful fabrication of the membranes, prototype solid-state proton batteries were assembled by integrating the electrolyte membrane with a MoO3 anode and a Prussian blue analogue (vanadium hexacyanoferrate, H-VHCF) cathode (Figure 4a).

The battery we developed using PA@ZVCOF-80 electrolyte achieved a record-high capacity of 108.5 mAh $\mathbf { g } ^ { - 1 }$ among all reported solid-state proton batteries, overcoming the low specific capacities suffered by many other systems.

text: Moreover, the solid-state electrolyte demonstrated lower corrosivity, which is advantageous for mitigating issues such as electrode degradation and current collector corrosion commonly encountered by proton batteries using liquid acid electrolytes.

To further highlight the advantages of our solid electrolyte, a comparative study was conducted using proton batteries assembled with a 5.0 M PA aqueous electrolyte, $\mathbf { M o O } _ { 3 }$ anode, and H-VHCF cathode.

In contrast, our solid-state system employing PA@ZVCOF-80 membranes preserved a much higher capacity of 76 mAh $\mathbf { g } ^ { - 1 }$ and achieved 84% retention even after 5000 cycles (Figures 5c and S35).

In conclusion, we have successfully synthesized a robust vinylene-linked zwitterionic COF that afforded a highperformance solid protonic electrolyte by encapsulating phosphoric acid within the COF channels.

Previous studies mainly focused on cast and wrought aluminum alloys that were originally designed for conventional processes [3,4].
The most widely studied aluminum alloys in LPBF were AlSi casting aluminum alloys, of which AlSi10Mg attracted the greatest attention [57].

Conventional alloys designed for cast and wrought processes cannot take full advantage of potential benefits brought by the high solidification rate of LPBF.

Thus, the research focus of LPBF aluminum alloys is gradually shifting from processing attempts on mature cast and wrought aluminum alloys to developing new aluminum alloy systems to accommodate unique thermomechanical conditions during the LPBF process.

Commercial cast and wrought aluminum alloys are unsuitable for structural applications above 200  due to the coarsening or dissolution of strengthening precipitates [1,2].

This creates a technological gap in lightweight alloys, which is presently being occupied by titanium alloys as they maintain both strength and stiffness at high temperatures better than aluminum alloys [3].

Laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) additive manufacturing technique provides an opportunity to design new aluminum alloys with high-temperature properties that cannot be achieved using conventional processing.

Three major groups of LPBF-fabricated aluminum alloys exhibit promise for high-temperature applications, i.e. high-temperature precipitation-strengthened aluminum alloys [9,10], aluminum alloys with a large volume fraction of intermetallics [1114], and aluminum alloys dispersed with ceramics [15,16].
Previous studies on aluminum alloys subjected to LPBF have primarily focused on Al-Si casting alloys [17], particularly AlSi10Mg.

Nevertheless, the substantial diffusivity of Si within the eutectic network in this alloy at elevated temperatures leads to rapid coarsening of precipitates, resulting in a decrease in strength above 200 °C [18,19].
This observation highlights the inherent limitations of conventional alloys in fully exploiting the potential advantages offered by LPBF for achieving high elevated-temperature strength.

Aluminum alloys specifically designed for LPBF have demonstrated enhanced strength at elevated temperatures through mechanisms such as solid solution strengthening [10,14], grain refinement [9,20], and dispersion strengthening via ceramics [9,20].
These compelling findings suggest the feasibility of designing novel aluminum alloys with exceptional high-temperature properties using LPBF technology.
We have developed an LPBF-fabricated Al-Cu-Li-Sc-Zr alloy exhibiting exceptional tensile properties at room temperatures [21].
The designed alloy falls under the category of high-temperature precipitation-strengthened aluminum aloys, with Sc and Zr contents surpassing their equilibrium solubilities [22,23].
The primary focus of this study lies in investigating the high-temperature mechanical properties of this novel alloy and elucidating their correlation with grain and precipitate thermal stability.

Consequently, our findings contribute to an enhanced understanding of the high-temperature behavior exhibited by the LPBF-fabricated Al-Cu-Li-Sc-Zr alloy, thereby facilitating the design of new aluminum alloys for potential applications at high temperatures.
A gas-atomized alloy powder, comprising Al-3.89Cu-1.22Li-0.98Sc-0.43Zr (wt%), was employed as the feedstock for the LPBF process using a LiM-X260A LPBF machine.
Two types of samples were selected: those in the as-fabricated (AF) condition and optimized heat-treated (HT) condition [24].
High-temperature tensile tests were performed on a Zwick/Roell Z020 Universal Materials Tester at three testing temperatures (200, 250, and 300 a).
The representative tensile curves of the AF and HT aluminum alloy samples at various testing temperatures are presented in Figure 1(a) and Figure 1(b).
The serrations observed in the room-temperature tensile stress-strain curve of Figure 1(a) can be explained by the Portevin-Le Chatelier (PLC) effect.
Consequently, this temperature-dependent behavior accounted for the absence of serrations in hightemperature tensile stress-strain curves.
The yield strength of AF sample decreased with the increase of testing temperature, while its elongation exhibited an opposite trend.

Aluminum alloys are favoured in the aerospace industry for the production of aircraft bodies and components due to their low density, high specific strength, and superior corrosion resistance [13].
The advancement of LPBF technology enables the production of complex aluminum alloy structures, fulfilling the demand for lightweight, high-performance aerospace designs [4- 8].
However, significant cracking issues associated with high-strength aluminum alloys, such as Al-Cu and Al-Zn, fabricated by LPBF have historically hindered their development.

Recent extensive studies indicate that heterogeneous nucleation methods, especially those involving Sc/Zr element modifications, effectively address the cracking problems while simultaneously enhancing the mechanical properties of the alloys [9- 12].

LPBF-fabricated Sc/Zr modified aluminum alloys exhibit distinct heterogeneous microstructural characteristics, which are directly related to the precipitation behaviour of primary $\mathsf { A l } _ { 3 } ( \mathsf { S c } , \mathsf { Z r } )$ phases under the specific solidification conditions [13].
The heterogeneous structure is significantly influenced by the content of Sc/Zr elements and the solidification conditions [14,15].

While the heterogeneous microstructure induced by Sc/Zr modification significantly enhances the strength of the alloy, the inherent brittleness of $\mathsf { A l } _ { 3 } ( \mathsf { S c } , \mathsf { Z r } )$ precipitates may constrain its plasticity, which is a common challenge in Sc/Zr modified high strength aluminum alloys.

To refine the grain size in the CG region and increase the overall volume fraction of FG, current research primarily focuses on modifying the alloy composition, particularly by increasing the content of the introduced Sc/Zr elements.

It results in the precipitation of $\mathsf { A l } _ { 3 } ( \mathsf { S c } , \mathsf { Z r } )$ phases in the already enriched FG region, manifesting as large, hard, and brittle particles that significantly degrade the ductility of the alloys [20,21].

Therefore, there is an upper limit to the amount of Sc/Zr that can be added, indicating that solely relying on elemental modification presents clear limitations in regulating the comprehensive mechanical properties of the alloy.

Regarding solidification conditions, adjusting process parameters, particularly reducing the solidification rate and preheating the substrate, can enhance the proportion of equiaxed grains to some extent.
While substrate preheating helps mitigate grain epitaxial growth by lowering temperature gradients, its effectiveness is limited [26].

In summary, pulsed laser provides point-level control, enhancing process flexibility and benefiting from higher cooling rates, which helps prevent overheating and reduce the risk of grain coarsening, allowing regulation of microstructure size and volume fraction.

Previous studies have shown that the fracture energies of Al-Sc and Al-Zr are greater than those of the aluminum matrix, and ${ \sf S c } / { \sf Z r }$ atoms readily doped into the matrix improve its strength [24].

While the addition of Sc/Zr elements significantly enhances the mechanical strength of the a-Al matrix, the resulting $\mathsf { A l } _ { 3 } ( \mathsf { L i } , \mathsf { S c } , \mathsf { Z r } )$ precipitates, which are hard and brittle, inevitably reduce ductility.
Additionally, as a typical precipitation-strengthened aluminum alloy, Al-Cu-Li alloys tend to experience a substantial sacrifice in ductility alongside strength gains after heat treatment.

However, the room temperature elongation of 4.82% in the CL sample indicates that while the synergy between strength and ductility in the heterogeneous structure of the Sc/Zr modified Al-Cu-Li alloy is effective, it is insufficient to offset the reduction in plasticity caused by the substantial precipitation of hard and brittle $\mathsf { A l } _ { 3 } ( \mathsf { L i } , \mathsf { S c } , \mathsf { Z r } )$ precipitates, revealing a limitation in enhancing ductility.

In this work, a remelting strategy was designed using pulsed laser to achieve fully equiaxed grain microstructures, ultimately doubling the elongation (4.82% for CL and 10.18% for PL) at the expense of a slight reduction in YS.

Owing to their high strength-to-weight ratio and excellent corrosion resistance, aluminum alloys are extensively used in fields such as aviation, aerospace, and transportation [1], playing a vital role in enhancing energy efficiency and reducing carbon emissions.
However, aluminum alloys exhibit poor thermal resistance, especially when compared to steels and titanium alloys  two other widely used metallic structural materials.
They suffer from a significant loss of strength with increasing temperature, are highly susceptible to creep at elevated temperatures, and possess poor microstructural thermal stability [2].
These factors present a major bottleneck, severely restricting the application of aluminum alloys in high-temperature environments.

Conventional approaches to enhancing the thermal resistance of aluminum alloys, as well as other metallic materials, principally rely on introducing a high density of finely dispersed second-phase particles into the metal matrix, either through alloy design coupled with heat treatment to induce in situ precipitation [3,4], or through external addition via techniques such as powder metallurgy [5,6].

The aluminum alloy developed via this strategy exhibits outstanding mechanical properties at both room and elevated temperatures, achieving a room-temperature ultimate tensile strength (\~676 MPa) among the highest reported for 3D-printed aluminum alloys, while demonstrating specific strengths that even surpass those of the Ti-6Al-4V titanium alloy up to 300°C.

It also displays highly sluggish creep behavior at elevated temperatures up to $4 0 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } ,$ with creep rates reduced by one or more orders of magnitude compared to other aluminum alloys, while retaining over 80% of its initial strength after prolonged hightemperature exposure (100 h at 300°C).
These attributes lead to a pronounced tendency for compositional undercooling during solidification [19], thereby providing a favorable thermodynamic driving force for amorphous phase formation.

Laser powder bed fusion (LPBF), a widely used additive manufacturing technique, was implemented to fabricate the alloy due to its high cooling rate (>105 K/s), which facilitates non-equilibrium solidification.

Aluminum alloys are known for their inherently low propensity to form amorphous phases [45], stemming from the thermodynamic instability of the undercooled liquid and the pronounced stability of the face-centered cubic crystalline phase [46].

These conditions are synergistically realized through the selection of alloy compositions with high solute element content and the use of an additive manufacturing process involving high cooling rates.

This approach eliminates the need for highly expensive Sc element additions which are commonly employed to facilitate heterogeneous nucleation through the in situ formation of nanoscale Al3Sc nucleants [10,25].

This is accompanied by an extremely low high-temperature creep rate, reduced by one to three orders of magnitude compared to most aluminum alloys under identical conditions, along with excellent thermal stability that retains over 80% of its strength after prolonged thermal exposure at 300°C for 100 h.

The exceptional synergy between the intrinsic properties of the alloy developed in this study and its processing advantages, including good printability, facile fabrication of intricate components, and near-netshape manufacturing, endows it with remarkable potential for hightemperature structural applications.

In summary, we propose a bioinspired nanoscale confinement strategy for strengthening materials from room to elevated temperatures, which contrasts from conventional dispersion strengthening, and validate its effectiveness in an additively manufactured aluminum alloy.

As a result, the alloy achieves an exceptional combination of properties surpassing those of conventional materials, including high room-temperature strength coupled with good ductility and work-hardening capability, excellent high-temperature strengths, superior creep resistance with creep rates orders of magnitude lower than those of counterparts, outstanding thermal stability, and good printability.

The new alloy design concepts, especially solute-induced dislocation-climb suppression for cree resitance, explored here may pave way for the design of new metallic alloys for thermal/electrical conductors and other high-temperature applications.
Batteries for electric vehicles (EVs) have increased the demand for alloys with an optimal combination of electrical conductivity (EC) and mechanical properties [1,2].

Rotors, inverters, stators, and busbars are among the EV applications requiring an improved combination of mechanical properties (strength, creep resistance, etc.) and EC for enhanced power output and efficiency of electric motors [1,3,4].
The high specific strength of Al alloys offers advantages over Cu alloys for improved driving range through lightweighting.

The maximum EC achievable in pure Al is \~65 % of that of coarse-grained pure Cu that has a resistivity of 58.1 MS/m at ${ } ^ { 2 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } }$ (defined as 100 % International Annealed Copper Standard (IASC) [4]).
The density of Al is however only 30 % that of Cu.
Achieving a combination of EC of 48 % IACS and a yield strength (YS) of 90140 MPa is the current threshold for EV applications [3].
The widely used Al-Si based A356 alloy has an EC of 40 % IACS, with its YS reaching as high as 225 MPa [2].

While some strengthening mechanisms, such as dislocation hardening, improve strength drastically with minimal conductivity loss  the approach well adopted for wrought Al conductor alloys  solutes in solid-solution reduce conductivity significantly with a marginal strength gain.

The precipitation hardening is the most effective strengthening mechanism in cast/wrought Al alloys, but solutes retained in solid-solution alongside the precipitates substantially deteriorate alloy conductivity [2].
Overcoming this tradeoff to maximize mechanical properties while minimizing the conductivity reduction requires new alloy design approaches.
Research efforts aimed at designing new Al-based conductor alloys have increased steadily in recent years.
Cast Al-2.7Ce-1.1Si-0.6Mg (wt. %) demonstrated a YS of 110 MPa and EC of 49 %IACS when heat treated to T5 or T6 temper [1].
Both these alloys derive their strength from metastable precipitates that are precursors to Mg2Si precipitates [1,2].
However, these precipitates coarsen rapidly at temperatures above 150 °C [6], making them unsuitable even for intermediate-temperature creep-relevant environments.

Fine, equiaxed $\mathrm { L 1 } _ { 2 ^ { - } } \mathrm { A l } _ { 3 } \mathrm { X }$ (X=Sc, Zr, etc.) nanoprecipitates, due to their high thermal stability, are popular candidates for improved thermal stability and creep resistance in Al alloys [7].
High solidification rates in AM can cause solute trapping which increases super-saturation beyond that of conventional processes.

For example, in a cast Al-0.054Fe (wt. %) alloy, \~0.04 wt. % Fe in solid solution achieved millionfold lower creep rates at 200 °C compared to when the Fe concentration in the α-Al matrix is only \~0.01 wt. % [18].
Small additions of other slow-diffusing solutes (e.g., Mn, Fe, Ti) also strongly reduce creep rates compared to pure Al [19].
A recent study [17] underscored the high efficiency of Mn in slowing the rate of dislocation climb in cast Al-Mn-Zr alloy.
However, Mn has a strong negative effect on electrical conductivity, almost twice that produced by Zr for a given concentration in the alloy [20].
AM processing enables extended Zr solute trapping in the α-Al matrix along with uniform solute distribution [21], which is difficult to achieve by casting processes.
Therefore, the feasibility of using Zr or other solute with slow diffusivity yet limited effect on conductivity to improve alloy creep resistance may be an effective design strategy.
Eutectic compositions with coarsening-resistant intermetallic particles have shown superior creep resistance to cast Al alloys in the 300400 °C range [16,22].
However, high fraction of such intermetallic particles alongside more solutes residing in α-Al lattice can lead to significant EC deterioration.
An attempt is made to balance this tradeoff in a recently introduced AM Al-1Fe-1Zr (wt. %) alloy to obtain a good combination of strength and thermal conductivity [23].

This study introduces a new, dilute Al-0.3Zr-0.2Ce-0.2Cu (wt. %) alloy, showing after rapid solidification via additive manufacturing (AM) an attractive combination of electrical conductivity and mechanical properties, especially creep resistance at intermediate temperatures.

Fig. 7a,b displays the temporal creep strain evolution curves of Al-Zr-Ce-Cu alloy at 200 °C in compression in the as-fabricated and two-stepaged states (Fig. 7).
Distinctly different creep performance is noted for as-fabricated and aged conditions.
The aged alloy is characterized by the development of typical primary and secondary creep at any given stress during multi-load compressive creep (Fig. 7a).
The dislocation storage and dynamic recovery are balanced following the primary creep that produces a measurable minimum secondary creep strain rate (Fig. 7a).
By contrast, the as-fabricated specimen shows some primary creep, but no measurable secondary creep (Fig. 7b).
The extent of primary creep is low up to \~65 MPa (i.e., up to alloy's yield point, Fig. 6b), but it becomes pronounced at higher stresses (Fig. 7b).

This observation indicates that the as-fabricated alloy has no, or limited, dynamic recovery, thus leading to the saturation of dislocation density for a given stress followed by complete suppression of dislocation creep.

The rationale behind the composition selection for this new Al-0.3Zr-0.2Ce-0.2Cu (wt. %) alloy is as follows.

Slow-diffusing Zr is known to improve alloy creep resistance through $\mathrm { L 1 } _ { 2 ^ { - } } \mathrm { A l } _ { 3 } \mathrm { Z r }$ precipitation [7,31, 32], while its limited solid solubility upon aging contributes to preserving the conductivity of the pure α-Al matrix.

Although the rapid solidification resulting from laser additive manufacturing allows for Zr supersaturation higher than 0.34 wt. % Zr (equivalent to 0.10 at. % Zr), this level of Zr addition was selected to study the feasibility of retarding dislocation climb (the mechanism that activates at elevated temperatures in Al alloys) while producing minimal conductivity loss.
Cerium also displays slow diffusivity and low solubility in α-Al.

Because Ce tends to react with Cu, Fe, Si and other typical impurities in Al alloys [33,34], Ce is expected to form, under rapid solidification conditions, highly refined intermetallic particles which also improve alloy strength and creep resistance as well as contributing to the higher level of conductivity of α-Al by scavenging impurities in solid solution.

The high solidification rates intrinsic to AM completely suppressed the formation of primary $\mathtt { A l _ { 3 } Z r }$ particles, which were expected from Scheil simulation of the alloy (Fig. 2b).
The regions right above the melt pool boundaries showed no (Ce,Cu)-rich intermetallic particles (Fig. 1c), forming particle-free zones consistent with initial epitaxial planar grain growth.

High thermal gradient (G) and low solidification (growth) rate (R), coupled with limited constitutional supercooling from low solute content in the alloy, are responsible for initial planar solidification [35,36].

The fact that as-fabricated Al-Zr-Ce-Cu alloy with Zr-solutestrengthened α-Al matrix shows no measurable secondary creep both below and above alloy yield point at $2 0 0 \ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C \ ( T / T _ { m } } \sim 0 . 5 )$ , as schematically illustrated in Fig. 12a, is surprising given the established fundamental knowledge on creep of Al alloys.

As noted for pure Al as well as for L12-Al3Zr-strenghened cast Al-Zr(-Sc) and aged AM Al-Zr-Ce-Cu alloys, dislocation climb becomes a rate-limiting mechanism, with its rate highly sensitive to the characteristics (size, etc.) of precipitates for Al alloys (Fig. 10b) [8,32,40].

Limited primary creep and near-zero secondary creep below alloy's yield point vs. large primary creep still with near-zero secondary creep (implying restricted dynamic recovery) above alloy's yield point (Fig. 7b) indicates complete suppression of dislocation climb during creep of the as-fabricated alloy.
Large primary-creep strain is obtained above alloy's yield point (Fig. 7b) because the moving dislocations tend to initially surmount (Ce,Cu)-rich particles by Orowan looping.
Some solutes in α-Al matrix are known to have a strong effect on dislocation climb process [17].

Sherby et al. [18] have shown that retaining \~0.04 wt. % Fe in α-Al matrix of cast Al-0.054Fe alloy leads to ${ 1 0 } ^ { 6 }$ times slower creep rates at 200 °C compared to when the Fe concentration in α-Al matrix is only \~0.01 wt. %.

Supersaturation of Mn in a L12-strengthened cast Al-Zr-Mn alloy leads to significantly lower creep rates at $3 0 0 { - } 4 0 0 \ { ^ { \circ } } \mathrm { C }$ compared to its Mn-free variant due to Mn-induced suppression of dislocation climb [17].

Our as-fabricated Al-Zr-Ce-Cu alloy has supersaturated Zr in α-Al matrix, which remained fully in solid solution (Table 6) and showed no sign of $\mathrm { L 1 } _ { 2 ^ { - } } \mathrm { A l } _ { 3 } \mathrm { Z r }$ precipitation during creep at 200 °C (Figs. 9e,i and Fig.
Based on these observations, we can infer that slow-diffusing Zr solutes in the α-Al matrix are most likely responsible for the suppression of dislocation climb in as-fabricated Al-Zr-Ce-Cu alloy.
The Al self-diffusivity is barely affected by minor Zr additions [49], which cannot account for the observed dislocation climb suppression.
More notable tracer diffusivity reduction requires much higher Zr concentration in solid solution than in our alloy (0.34 wt. % Zr).
A 23x tracer diffusivity reduction has been estimated using Molecular $\mathrm { D y } \cdot$ namics modelling for Al-17 wt. % Zr solid-solution alloy relative to pure Al [49].

Because dislocation glide occurs for our alloy when the stress level is high enough, as noted from high primary-creep strains (Fig. 7b) and the presence of numerous matrix dislocations (Fig. 9ek), the near-zero secondary creep both below and above alloy's yield strength points towards complete suppression of dislocation climb via the formation of a Cottrell atmosphere.
Although Zr solute has lower interaction energy of 0.14 eV with dislocation [17], increased Zr supersaturation due to rapid cooling enables Zr diffusion to the core of edge dislocation.
Based on the first-principles calculations in Ref. [17] and reproduced in Fig. 11b, Zr tends to segregate to the tensile-deformed region of the edge dislocation.

According to recent first-principles density functional calculations [51,52], Zr prefers to form $\mathrm { Z r - Z r }$ pair in the second nearest neighbor (2NN) position rather than in the first nearest neighbor (1NN).
These results indicate that it is energetically favorable for vacancy to form Zr  vacancy pair, particularly Zr  Zr  vacancy pair.
Trapping of vacancies by Zr atoms near the core of edge dislocations is another possible explanation for the dislocation-climb-restricted creep behavior of our as-fabricated Al-Zr-Ce-Cu alloy.

A plausible explanation for how such pairing can affect dislocation climb is the entrapment of vacancies by Zr near or at the core of dislocations, thus restricting vacancy flow (at a level) required for the positive or negative climb process to occur.

In an earlier study [54], a favorable Zr solute - vacancy binding energy measured experimentally in Al-Zr alloy has, indeed, led to the conclusion that Zr traps vacancies by forming pairs and prevents vacancy condensation into dislocation loops.

When such Zr solute - vacancy pairs control the climb rate, diffusivity of Zr in the Al lattice, rather than self-diffusion, becomes the rate limiting step that controls vacancy diffusion at or near dislocation cores.

This hypothesis is also consistent with the findings of Sherby et al. [18] on cast Al-0.054Fe alloy, where retaining \~0.04 wt. % Fe in α-Al matrix leads to a dramatically slower creep rates at $2 0 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ (by a factor $1 0 ^ { 6 } )$ compared to when the Fe concentration in α-Al matrix is only \~0.01 wt. % and that the activation energy for creep equals that of Fe diffusion in α-Al matrix only for the former alloy condition.

Energetically favorable solute interaction with dislocations, along with limited solute diffusivity in Al matrix and a sufficiently high concentration in Al matrix all must be fulfilled for the solute to be effective at suppressing dislocation climb in a certain temperature range [17].

A solute-lean Al-0.3Zr-0.2Ce-0.2Cu (wt. %) alloy composition was designed in this study to maximize the solubility of Zr in α-Al, while avoiding primary $\mathrm { A l _ { 3 } Z r }$ phase formation because extended solid solubility of Zr ensures improved combination of strength and conductivity.
The benefits of adding Ce to the alloy is twofold.
It scavenges common impurities in Al alloys, such as Cu, Fe, and Si, and it forms fine, numerous (Ce,Cu)-rich intermetallic particles with high strengthening effects.

Owing to the limited solubility and slow diffusivity of Ce in α-Al, these intermetallic particles remain coarsening-resistant during alloy aging at $3 7 5 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ (which is performed to produce L1 $\mathbf { \varepsilon } _ { 2 } { \cdot } \mathbf { A l } _ { 3 } \mathbf { Z r }$ precipitates), hence maintaining the compatibility between Zr and Ce for maximized contribution of each component.

Indeed, the aged $_ { \mathrm { A l - Z r - C e - C u } }$ alloy exhibits attractive properties: with a YS of \~150 MPa, a conductivity of \~58 %IACS, and a high creep resistance at $2 0 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ with limited dislocation creep below \~40 MPa, this alloy shows promise for conductor applications.

A new strategy of fully suppressing dislocation creep at stresses up to alloy's YS, which we achieve here by supersaturating slow-diffusing Zr in α-Al matrix, represents a conceptual change in conductor alloy design for creep-relevant environments.

A conductivity of \~48 %IACS even when all Zr remains in solid solution and the feasibility of achieving such unprecedented creep resistance at even lower Zr levels (which translates into higher EC values) provide new pathways for designing highly creep resistant Al conductor alloys needed in a wide variety of applications, such as rotors, inverters, busbars, windings, heat exchangers/sinks.

Although such improvement may be expected by adding other slowdiffusing transition metals (e.g., Ti, Mn, and V), Zr stands out among these elements due to its least negative effect on alloy conductivity, on a wt. % basis.

Such homogeneity is intrinsically challenging to achieve in cast alloys due to heavy Zr segregation to α-Al grain cores due to its peritectic reaction and the large equilibrium partitioning coefficient for α-Al solidification [32,56].

Homogeneous Zr distribution in AM Al-Zr-Ce-Cu alloy enables the suppression of dislocation climb throughout the grain interiors and avoids the formation of locally weak regions (links) which otherwise limit the creep resistance and lifetime in this alloy system [12,13,15].

All-solid-state batteries (SSBs) have become an exciting energy storage technology to replace conventional lithium-ion batteries.[1,2] They improve safety by removing organic carbonate-based liquid electrolytes and can potentially increase energy density by utilizing a Li-metal anode.[3] However, while proof of concept of SSBs has been shown, multiple hurdles still have to be overcome before they can truly compete with today's commercialized Li-ion cells in terms of energy density[4 In this paper, we focus on active material loading in the cathode as one of these challenges.

Nickel-based superalloys, which exhibit excellent comprehensive mechanical properties, are critical materials for the hottest sections of advanced aero-engines and industrial gas turbines [1].
However, the requirement of extreme service performance places very strict requirements on the temperature capacity of superalloys [2,3].
On the other hand, the evolution of superalloys, from polycrystalline to single crystal (SX), with completely eliminated grain boundaries, yields further improved temperature capacity.
Compositional optimization is a basic route for developing highperformance superalloys [812].

The first, second and third generation SX superalloys have been developed and classified in terms of their Re contents (0 wt.%, \~3 wt.%, and \~6 wt.%) and different contents of Al, Ti, and refractory elements, including Mo, W, and Ta [1315].
As a crucial element, Re is strongly partitioned in the γ matrix, and has a very low diffusion coefficient.

However, the increase in Re content is not only detrimental for lightweight component design but also causes microstructural instabilities, including the formation of topologically close-packed (TCP) phases and secondary reaction zones, which are detrimental to long-term service performance at elevated temperatures [18,19].
Consequently, high cost is another factor that limits Re additions in superalloys and its widespread application.
Recently, much attention has been paid to the development of advanced SX superalloys with lower Re or no Re content.

QTSX alloy [21], developed by QuesTek Innovations, contains only 1 wt.% Re and exhibits superior castability and similar or better high-temperature mechanical properties compared to the widely used SX superalloys, such as PWA 1484 and René N5.
Cannon-Muskegon reported the Re-free CMSX-7 alloy and low-Re CMsx-8 alloy [22] (1.5 wt.% Re) as alternatives to the first and second generation SX superalloys for applications, respectively.

In certain Re-free Ni-based superalloys, the distribution of the refractory element W between the $\gamma$ and $\gamma ^ { \prime }$ phases can be influenced by Ti additions [13,23,24], and then, the alloy creep strengths at elevated temperatures can be enhanced due to the higher solid solution strengthening effect.
For example, the creep strain rate of the ERBO/36-Ti alloy (1 at.% Ti) was increased compared to that of Astra100 (Ti-free) at 1100 C [13].

In contrast, previous studies have tended to eliminate the Ti element in the modern SX superalloys due to its negative effects on oxidation resistance and the retention of thermal barrier coatings (TBCs) [1,26,27].
However, Guan et al. [32] indicated that the increase in Ti content improves the hot corrosion resistance.
Thus, the Ti concentration should be limited in Ni-based SX superalloys, considering the potential benefits to alloy strength and the adverse effects on environmental resistance.
The Ti-containing alloy exhibited significantly enhanced creep performance.
We believe that the study results will provide a new approach to further improve the temperature capacity of nickel-based SX superalloys and reduce alloy cost and density.

Nevertheless, the broad application of LPBF-manufactured Ti-6Al-4V alloys has encountered a notable strength-ductility compromise.
Therefore, optimizing both the process and post-heat treatment (HT) parameters to successfully balance strength and ductility is critical for meeting performance demands.

This effect is attributed to the increased thermal retention in the melt pool, which facilitates the alignment of dendrites parallel to the thermal flux, consequently fostering the development of columnar crystals.

Therefore, both LPBF process parameters and post-HT conditions must be considered to comprehensively understand process-property relationships and to optimize mechanical properties of additive manufactured Ti-6Al-4V alloys.

Experimentally, a large number of iterative experiments have been conducted based on the design of experiments (DoE) method and, computationally, various properties of Ti-6Al-4V alloys have been explored through simulations to identify combinations that can yield the desired properties of alloys.

While these experimental and computational studies have successfully produced alloys with the desired mechanical properties, vast number of combinations worth exploring still exist due to the time and resource limitations of both methods32.

Specifically, Akbari et al.36 used ML to predict the yield strength, UTS, and elastic modulus of additively manufactured components, while Zhan et al.37 developed an ML model to predict the fatigue life of stainless steel 316 L using additive manufacturing process parameters as input features.

For every active learning iteration, two new combinations of LPBF process parameters and HT conditions were selected to produce the corresponding Ti-6Al-4V alloy specimens, with their UTS and TE values obtained through tensile tests.

The proposed Pareto active learning framework whose efficiency and effectiveness are demonstrated throughout this study is expected to enable precise and efficient tailoring of LPBF-fabricated Ti-6Al-4V alloys to meet diverse application requirements.

A total of 119 combinations of LPBF process parameters and post-HT conditions were extracted from previous studies43-57, , and the UTS and TE of Ti-6Al-4V alloys fabricated using each combination were recorded.

Before implementing the Pareto active learning framework, pairwise plots (Fig. 2) were generated using the initial dataset to determine whether combinations of LPBF process parameters and post-HT conditions that can produce Ti-6Al-4V alloys with high UTS and TE could be designed based solely on the pairwise relationships between each parameter and mechanical properties, and to understand the individual effects of LPBF process parameters and post-HT conditions on UTS and TE.

Corroborating the trends identified in Fig. 2a, the Ti-6Al-4V samples with the top 10% TE values were fabricated with high values for all three parameters, whereas those with the top 10% UTS were fabricated with low values.
This implies that it is essential to consider synergistic effects between them for fabricating Ti-6Al-4V alloys with both high UTS and TE.

Hence, the framework accurately pinpointed the combinations capable of fabricating Ti-6Al-4V alloys with higher TE at comparable UTS levels and vice versa, thus demonstrating the possibility of improving one property without significantly compromising the other.

The third iteration further expanded the Pareto front as presented in Fig. 4c, identifying combinations that resulted in Ti-6Al-4V alloys with a 3.5% point increase in TE and a 125 MPa improvement in UTS compared with the updated training dataset comprising known 123 combinations.

Remarkably, except for the 5-2 sample, the UTS and TE values of the remaining 9 combinations of Ti-6Al-4V alloys, identified by the Pareto active learning framework, not only surpassed those in the initial dataset of 119 combinations used for the framework but also exhibited superior performance compared to the properties of Ti-6Al-4V alloys reported in previous studies on directed energy deposition (DED)-processed and wrought Ti-6Al-4V alloys, as illustrated in Fig. 4f.

Consequently, it was demonstrated that the Pareto active learning framework proposed in this study effectively investigated unknown combinations of LPBF process parameters and post-HT conditions, expeditiously and accurately identifying combinations that yielded Ti-6Al-4V alloys with high strength and ductility.

IN718 superalloy exhibits outstanding mechanical, chemical, and thermal properties, including high-temperature strength, thermal stability, corrosion resistance, fatigue resistance, and radiation resistance [1].
It finds extensive applications in extreme environments across various industries, such as aerospace, automotive, marine, petrochemical, and nuclear energy [2].
These attributes also pose challenges for machining, resulting in a notable decrease in the machinability index of IN718 superalloy [3].

Cryogenic machining effectively responds to the above challenge, which utilizes liquid nitrogen and carbon dioxide to control the machining temperature [4,5], avoiding workpiece burn and minimizing tool wear [6].
High-pressure jet assisted machining significantly boosts the convective heat transfer coefficient [7], through enhancing coolant diffusion [8].
In addition, thermal conductive coating also plays a positive role in making up for the problem of low conductivity [9].

However, compared to methods like using cryogenic coolant and thermal conductive coating during machining, suppressing heat generation at the source is more advantageous for extending tool life and enhancing the continuity of machining [10].
Minimum Quantity Lubrication (MQL) is a typical method through creating dense lubricant films on the tool-workpiece and tool-chip surfaces.
To improve the lubrication performance, solid lubricant-assisted MQL [11] and nanofluid-assisted MQL [12] have been introduced.
Based on the above analysis, auxiliary processes are commonly employed to enhance the machinability of IN718 superalloy.

However, the addition of lubrication, cooling and preheating devices increases the complexity of the production process and the uncertainty of industrial control, which is not conducive to the economy and green sustainability.

Additively manufactured (AM) aluminum (Al) alloys with high strength at elevated service temperatures (e.g., ≈150- 400 °C) can find broad industrial applications in components of jet engines, combustion engines, vacuum pumps, and more.[1] Laser-based AM, particularly laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) that operates under non-equilibrium conditions due to rapid solidification, can endow the alloy products with microstructural features that are challenging to attain via conventional near-equilibrium liquid metallurgy routes.

One of the outstanding benefits of rapid solidification is the metastable phases that can effectively modulate the macroscopic physical and/or mechanical properties of as-built or heat-treated alloys.

Two strategies are commonly employed to strengthen Al alloys1: employing precipitates, especially with L12 structures, is the first main strategy,[8] and segmenting grains by laminated eutectic phases to further impede dislocation motion1.
These two factors were considered in the present alloy design (Figure 4a,f, Results and Discussion: Step IV).
Certain elements in the periodic table promote L12 formation during casting or rapid solidification of AM.
Besides all conditions for high-temperature strengthening, it is required that the Al alloys be printable (defined as remaining crack-free during solidification).
Defects during rapid solidification of AM can be of two types: processing defects or solidification defects.
The design approach was demonstrated by performing a full alloy design cycle of a model Al alloy (Al-Er-Zr-Y-Yb-Ni) for AM, spanning from virtual predictions to experimental validation (Figure 5a).
